extracted.intended_audience: readers of fact-checking journalism; journalists and media professionals interested in retraction/correction practices
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and reporting on a news publication's retraction/ correction practices and the factual accuracy of a disputed article (here, a COVID-19 deaths piece). Focus is on whether the article's claims, sourcing, statistical presentation, and the publisher's handling met journalistic standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: When retracting or unpublishing content, the publication should explain how and why the decision was made and provide access to the original material for reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The News-Letter published an editorial update explaining its decision and shared a link to the original article as a PDF with an overlay reading “Retracted by The News-Letter.” The update described the reasoning (inaccurately reported key points that contributed to misinformation) and provided archived links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt correction policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Quickly correct errors of fact and clarify potentially confusing or ambiguous statements; document substantive changes publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Snopes's policy: 'promptly correct errors of fact and to clarify any potentially confusing or ambiguous statements in our articles. Whenever we correct or modify a substantive supporting fact or add substantial new information to an existing article, those changes are noted and explained in an “update” box at the foot of the article.' Use an update box or similar transparent note for significant edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding spread of misinformation as retraction justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Retract or unpublish pieces when key points are inaccurately reported and contribute to the spread of misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The News-Letter said it retracted to 'stop the spread of misinformation.' Retraction is appropriate when content reasonably fuels false narratives or dangerous inaccuracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide and link to primary data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles making empirical claims should include links to the underlying data cited so readers can verify analyses and numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disputed article did not link to the data it described; Snopes and Johns Hopkins data contradicted some claims. Best practice: link to CDC, Johns Hopkins, or other primary datasets used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize single-study or single-presenter claims within broader evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present one study, webinar, or presenter as sufficient to understand a large public-health issue; place findings in context with other authoritative sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The News-Letter editors noted Briand’s study 'should not be used exclusively' and should be taken in context with data from Hopkins, WHO, and CDC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of expert credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure conclusions about specialized topics (e.g., disease impact) rely on appropriately qualified experts; disclose relevant qualifications or lack thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editors pointed out Briand is 'neither a medical professional nor a disease researcher.' Publications should disclose the presenter’s credentials and avoid overstating conclusions from non-experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for raw death counts and excess-death estimates when claiming 'no excess deaths'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that COVID-19 did not create excess deaths must consider spikes in raw death counts and authoritative excess-death estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The News-Letter retraction cited a spike in raw death counts and the CDC estimate of ~299,028 excess U.S. COVID-19 deaths (Jan–Oct 3) as evidence that the original claim overlooked key measures; articles should use raw numbers and recognized excess-death methodologies when making such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading statistical presentation (proportions vs raw numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting COVID-19 deaths as a proportion of all deaths can trivialize the pandemic’s impact; use raw numbers and appropriate metrics to convey severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editors criticized presenting total deaths as percentages rather than raw numbers because proportionality can obscure increases in absolute death counts. Guidance: show both raw counts and rates where relevant and explain implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and disclose editorial independence / conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear whether publication content is endorsed by affiliated institutions and whether editorial decisions are independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The News-Letter explicitly stated it is 'editorially and financially independent' and that articles are not endorsed by the University or School of Medicine; such disclosures help readers evaluate potential institutional influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh transparency against removal — prefer documented corrections/archives
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize debate that removing misreported content can reduce transparency and credibility; when possible, document corrections rather than silently deleting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites groups (Society of Professional Journalism, The Pointer Institute) arguing that removal reduces transparency. Best practice: if content is retracted, provide archived copies, clear retraction notices, and editorial explanation instead of silent deletion.
